title: Whoever else leaps my walls
saying: sīc deinde, quīcumque alius trānsiliet moenia mea
author: Livy

source_text: inde cum altercatione congressi certamine irarum ad caedem vertuntur; ibi in turba ictus Remus cecidit. vulgatior fama est ludibrio fratris Remum novos transiluisse muros; inde ab irato Romulo, cum verbis quoque increpitans adiecisset "sic deinde, quicumque alius transiliet moenia mea," interfectum.
excerpt_note: Section 1.7.2 complete: Livy's two versions of Remus's death. The edition does not capitalize the first word of a sentence, and neither does this text; its curly quotation marks are given here as straight ones. The Perseus file's own header warns that its OCR correction "appears poor and many misprints remain", so this text was compared word for word with Perseus's digital texts of the Loeb edition (B. O. Foster, 1919/1922; file perseus-lat4) and the Oxford edition (Conway and Walters; file perseus-lat3). Both agree word for word; the Oxford text spells volgatior and puts a comma before the quotation, and the Loeb text begins section 2 a sentence earlier.

translation: Then they came to blows in a wrangle, and the contest of their anger turns to bloodshed; there, in the crush, Remus was struck and fell. The more widespread story is that Remus, to mock his brother, jumped over the new walls, and that he was then killed by the angry Romulus, who added these taunting words as well: "So perish, from now on, anyone else who jumps over my walls!"
translation_note: The threat is elliptical: sīc deinde, quīcumque alius trānsiliet moenia mea has no main verb, and something like pereat, "may he perish", is understood. The whole second sentence depends on fāma est, "the story is", so it is indirect statement (Remum ... trānsiluisse; interfectum [esse]): Livy reports a tale, he does not vouch for it. vertuntur is a vivid present in the middle of past tenses.

essay.t: Livy's preface admits that the traditions about the time before Rome was founded are adorned more by poets' tales than by trustworthy records, and says he means neither to affirm nor to refute them.
Antiquity, he adds, is allowed to mingle the human with the divine to make the beginnings of cities more august.
In his story the usurper Amulius has the newborn twins put into the flooded Tiber; stranded on dry ground, they are suckled by a thirsty she-wolf until the king's herdsman Faustulus finds them.

Livy at once offers a rationalizing alternative: some think that Faustulus's wife Larentia was called lupa, "she-wolf", among the shepherds because she sold her body, and that this gave the fable its start.
To settle who would name and rule their new city, the twins took the auspices, Romulus on the Palatine, Remus on the Aventine.
Remus reportedly saw six vultures first, Romulus twelve later, and each side hailed its man as king.
Livy then gives two versions of Remus's death: struck down in the brawl that followed, or, in the "more widespread" story of the passage, killed by Romulus for jumping over the new walls in mockery.
The famous threat belongs only to the second version, which the grammar reports as hearsay; that reading is my own.

Britannica treats Romulus as an invention of later historians, adapted from a folktale told of many Mediterranean founders, and notes that ancient dates for the founding ranged from 814 to 728 BC before 753 became accepted.
Archaeology, it says, confirms an early village of thatched huts on the Palatine but dates its beginning to the 10th or 9th century BC.

In 2005 Andrea Carandini presented an 8th-century building near the shrine of Vesta as "a palace fit for a king"; Elizabeth Fentress of the British School at Rome replied that nothing tied it to Romulus.

Even the bronze she-wolf in Rome's Capitoline Museums is no ancient witness: radiocarbon tests reported in 2012 dated its casting to between about 1021 and 1153, and the twins were added in the Renaissance.

questions.q: How does Livy say Remus died?
options: He gives two versions: in a brawl, or (the more common story) killed by Romulus for jumping the new walls
He drowned in the Tiber as a baby
He ruled jointly with Romulus and died old

questions.q: What rationalizing explanation of the she-wolf does Livy report?
options: Some thought Larentia was called lupa by the shepherds because she sold her body
The wolf was really a dog
The story was invented by Augustus
The wolf was a statue on the Palatine

questions.q: What did the 2012 radiocarbon tests suggest about the Capitoline she-wolf?
options: It was cast in the Middle Ages, about 1021–1153
It is an Etruscan work of the 5th century BC
It dates from the founding of Rome
The twins are part of the original casting
